prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms confined at the magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as my whole prize, and the chair's first question gives me the chance to put the distinctness argument in one sentence. The 2005 comb prize gave us a way to count optical cycles. The 2012 prize gave us control of a single quantum system, one ion with its small signal. The lattice clock showed that thousands of neutral atoms can be held in light and interrogated together, with the trapping light itself cancelled out of the transition frequency at the magic wavelength, so that the large-ensemble signal-to-noise advantage is gained without giving up ion-level control of systematic shifts. That is a physical insight about light shifts, not only a better apparatus, and it is the reason the many-atom clocks now reach the 1e-18 level and are used to study interactions and many-body effects between the atoms in the lattice. The result is well reproduced: several independent national and university laboratories build such clocks and compare them with each other, and they agree at that level. That is the kind of independent confirmation I weigh most, and it is stronger for B001 than for any other shortlisted item I can judge. The credit is two names with a clear division, Katori for the proposal and first realisation and Ye for taking the scheme to the accuracy and many-body frontier. After reading everyone's round 1, I have not been given a scientific reason to move. I have been given a good reason to tighten the citation, so that it names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength idea and does not mention records or applications.
statement.case_against: The distinctness question is still the real risk, and the clearest answer to it is a judgement, not a proof. Members who read the comb, the ion clock and the lattice clock as one precision-timekeeping lineage will see a refinement, and I cannot show them otherwise by argument alone. Two names leave out Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto, Bloom and others, and I accept that this is a genuine cost, not a small one. The redefinition of the second has not happened, which some will read as a reason to wait. Finally, topological insulators have the widest support in the committee, and I should not treat my own first place as if it carried more scientific weight than the breadth of the B024 ranking. If the committee decides that B024 can be given a fair allocation, I would not obstruct it on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Danielsson says he could rank lattice clocks first if the committee can state what the lattice clock showed beyond the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes, and he moved to B024 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) after reading the opening ballots.
responses.response: Here is my attempt at the sharper statement you asked for. The magic-wavelength condition is the new fact: a trap that does not shift the clock transition, so a large ensemble can be used, which a single ion cannot offer, and which the comb alone does not provide. I do not claim it is a discovery of the same type as nature supplying a clue, as with IceCube, which you value. It is an invention, and the statutes name inventions. I also want to say plainly that I think your B024 configuration is serious, and that your point about a defensible trio is the one that decides it. If condensed-matter colleagues can settle between Mele and Hasan with a reason that does not leave Mele, who co-wrote the founding papers, out of a Kane prize, I would find that a better answer than my own. I would still say the unresolved Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question makes B024 harder to defend than a clean two-name award.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps Mele with Kane because the two wrote the founding papers on the Z2 invariant, and anchors the prize on Molenkamp's observation of the quantum spin Hall state, while acknowledging that Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are left out.
responses.response: I agree with you that splitting Kane and Mele would be wrong, and I think your reasoning is more compelling than the alternative of replacing Mele by Hasan. Given that, the honest accounting is that B024 on your trio recognises the 2D quantum spin Hall effect and its prediction, and leaves the 3D observation and the HgTe proposal outside. Johansson is right that this is a cost, and I think the citation would then have to say precisely 'quantum spin Hall' and not 'topological insulators' in general. That makes the claim narrower than the breadth of the field you describe, which is the main source of its appeal. By comparison the clock citation can be exact without any gap between what it says and what the two laureates did. I have not changed my position, but I would not vote against B024 on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, pairs lattice clocks with IceCube (Halzen alone), calls the single-name credit for a collaboration his weakest link, and says he would prefer B024 as the main prize if condensed-matter colleagues find a fair allocation.
responses.response: I think you have identified the problem yourself, and I want to take your own words seriously. Pairing two achievements gives a three-person prize, but the second part would credit one person for a discovery made by a collaboration of hundreds and with predecessors in AMANDA and DUMAND, and several colleagues have raised that. If the diffuse flux were the cited result I would still want to hear which decisive contribution is Halzen's. I would also not like the clock to be paired with something only to fill out a configuration, since that would make the pair look like a compromise. I prefer B001 as a single part. If you decide the IceCube credit cannot be defended, your own stated fallback, B024, and my own are not far apart as options, and I would rather the committee make that choice than add an uncertain second part.

responses.point: Olsson wants the clock citation to avoid practical-impact language and to keep to the measurement regime that was opened, noting that records will be broken and that the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I accept that and have changed the citation accordingly: it now names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength confinement and says nothing about the redefinition of the second, gravitational redshift or any record figure. On timing, I take the redefinition to be a consequence of the achievement and not a precondition for it, and I think this is the right place to say so. The achievement has already been established by independent comparison among laboratories, whether or not the metrology bodies decide to redefine the second this decade or the next. I do have one disagreement with your framing of the credit. You describe the division between the proposal, the first demonstration and the accuracy work as hard to verify. I think the division is clear enough for two names, and the real cost lies with the uncredited groups who made the clocks reliable, which is a question of limits on the number of laureates and not a problem of attribution within the pair.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and says he cannot judge from solid-state physics whether lattice clocks carry a distinct physical discovery beyond instrumentation, and also doubts a five-name ultracold-atom simulation credit.
responses.response: On your question about whether the clock is more than instrumentation, I would offer the same answer as to Danielsson, that the magic-wavelength condition is a physics result about light shifts, and the clock is the demonstration. I also respect your point that twisted bilayer graphene has been reproduced by many groups for the phenomena, which I think is true and is the strongest part of your case. My difficulty is the one that Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson and you yourself raise: eight years, an unsettled pairing mechanism, twist-angle disorder, and a choice among four names that leaves out someone with a real claim. I would put it as a candidate for a coming year, not this one. On ultracold-atom simulation (B041), I keep it only as an alternative, since the five-name credit cannot be cut to three without losing a decisive contributor, though I think the science is mature.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes. I have given my best one-sentence answer, but this is a judgement that other members are entitled to make differently.
Whether leaving out Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto and Bloom can be justified as the price of a two-name prize.

Whether the pending redefinition of the second should weigh for, against or not at all. I read it as a consequence of the achievement and not a requirement for it, but I am not certain the committee will agree.
Whether the B024 allocation problem (Mele or Hasan, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside the list) has a defensible resolution that I, as an atomic theorist, am not placed to judge.
I have not verified current clock uncertainty figures or the exact status of the redefinition roadmap, so the citation says only that a new regime of precision was opened.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I have no connection to Katori or Ye and none to the credited names of any other shortlisted ballot that I know of from my profile. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and ETH Zurich attosecond groups, but none of them are credited on this shortlist. My atomic-structure and many-body background makes me sympathetic to B001, B041 and B029, and I have kept B001 as my choice with that in mind. As Kroll and I both declared field proximity on B001, I would support the chair treating our two votes as informed but not independent of that background, and I note that I am willing to consider B024 if a defensible allocation emerges. I have deferred to colleagues on particle, astroparticle and condensed-matter questions.
